prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

be built and design properly to allow for easy walking. Those include the presence and continuity of sidewalks and pedestrian routes that connect pedestrians to frequent transit services with safe crossings (Hutabarat Lo, 2009). In addition, the place should also provide accessibility of facilitate people with different abilities. Based on the above discussions, it is apparent that the environmental quality and the physical arrangement of urban elements are influential in providing pedestrian comfort. For the purpose of this study, physical attributes and condition are examined to understand the impact of walkability attributes on pedestrian’s comfort of walking. 2.3. Connectivity and accessibility Connectivity and accessibility are important criteria for pedestrian comfort (Hutabarat Lo, 2009; Vojnovic, 2006). Connectivity relates to the ease of moving from origins to destinations is the major factor influencing the pedestrian route choice (Kumar, 2010). The street networks need to be well connected with proper sidewalks to varied destination to encourage people to walk in the city. A well-planned street network has streets that are well linked to other modes of transportation (Southworth, 2005). The streets should also provide varied uses of buildings and spaces, good quality of paths, adequate width of walkways, clear signage. The street design creates the visual interest of the built environment. All of these elements are important to facilitate walking with ease. Accessibility is an important factor for walkability. A place is accessible when there is an equal opportunity for everybody to use public spaces. A normal person can be disabled if accessibility is not provided. On the other hand, even a wheelchair user, a blind person or an elderly are not disabled in an accessible environment. Street with a large amount of frontages taken up by parking makes pedestrian access to buildings more difficult by requiring pedestrians to cross the parking lot. According to Handy, Xinyu and Mokhtarian (2006), different physical settings may affect the walking pattern and route choice. For example, pedestrians who choose to walk may consider the distance to the destination as important to reduce the time consumed. They will prefer a place that has short walking distance and high connectivity walkways. In one way, the distance of walking should be minimized and connectivity should be maintained in order to reduce the time and cost of travel. The scholar suggests that proximity, connectivity and accessibility are significant criteria in encouraging walking activity. In this respect, this study highlights the current condition and accessibility of facilities, proximity of the places and continuity of the walkways in providing physical comfort and pleasant walking for visitor as pedestrians. 2.4. Safety of walking Safety is one of the determinants of a walkable environment. A safe pedestrian environment allows the pedestrians to walk comfortably and reduces the sense of fear from accident or crime. Southworth (2005) claimed that the quality of the walking environment might influence pedestrian intensity. The intensity of pedestrian is required to increase safety because the places become more transparent (Jacobs, 1969).       "The street space is dominated by a single narrow carriageway with only very limited edge walking space, so spatial resources are distributed more toward vehicles than toward pedestrians.",
      "Both sides show hard edges—a long blank wall on the left and walled residential frontages on the right—which provide little visible public amenity such as seating, marked pedestrian zones, or shared-use facilities for different users.",
      "Accessibility is only moderate because the roadside margins appear mostly flat, but there are no clearly marked sidewalks, curb ramps, tactile paving, or designated crossings visible for inclusive use by all social groups."
    ],
    "safety": [
      "Motor traffic appears low because the road is narrow, residential, and nearly empty, which likely reduces conflict risk for all road users.",
      "A centerline is visible and the pavement surface looks newly maintained, helping lane discipline and reducing tripping or cycling hazards from potholes.",
      "Safety is limited by the absence of separated sidewalks or bike lanes, meaning pedestrians and cyclists would need to share space directly with vehicles on the carriageway."
    ],
    "livability": [
      "The street is quiet and clean, with little clutter, litter, or visible heavy traffic, which supports a calm residential atmosphere.",
      "Large trees and low-rise buildings create a pleasant neighborhood character, but there are few visible active frontages, shops, or community facilities that would support everyday street life.",
      "The long blank wall on the left reduces social interaction and visual engagement, making the corridor feel less lively despite its orderly appearance."
    ],
    "sustainability": [
      "The mature tree canopy over the roadway is a strong positive feature, contributing shade, cooling, and ecological value.",
      "The compact residential form and low-speed local street pattern can support short local trips, but no visible transit stop, bike parking, or dedicated cycling infrastructure is present.",
      "Most visible surfaces are paved with asphalt or concrete, and there are no obvious rain gardens, permeable strips, or other stormwater features in view."
    ],
    "aesthetics": [
      "The overhanging tree canopy frames the street and gives the scene a strong visual identity.",
      "The street appears clean and orderly, with simple low-rise buildings and a consistent wall line that create visual coherence.",
      "Aesthetic quality is reduced somewhat by the long blank wall on the left, which adds monotony even though it is well maintained."
    ],
    "comfort": [
      "Thermal comfort is relatively good because the large roadside trees provide substantial shade over much of the street.",
      "Physical comfort is mixed: the asphalt surface looks smooth, but there are no clearly defined sidewalks, benches, or resting places visible.",
      "Psychological comfort is fairly good for all road users because the street appears quiet, low-traffic, and uncrowded, though the blank wall may feel less engaging for pedestrians."
    ],
    "walkability": [
      "Walkability is constrained because there is no clearly continuous, dedicated sidewalk separated from the travel lane on either side.",
      "The roadside margins appear mostly level and unobstructed in places, which helps basic walking movement, but driveway cuts and narrow edge space reduce pedestrian priority.",
      "Shade from the mature trees improves walking comfort, yet the lack of crossings, pedestrian markings, and active destinations limits the street's overall walking appeal."
    ]
  }
}

Shade from the mature trees improves walking comfort, yet the lack of crossings, pedestrian markings, and active destinations limits the street's overall walking appeal.

As a city streetscape evaluation expert, please analyze the uploaded streetscape image based on the specified persona perspective and evaluation indicators, and return a JSON result.
 Persona Selection
Road User Type
- All Road Users
- Pedestrians
- Cyclists
- Drivers
Socially Vulnerable Groups
- All Social Groups
- Persons with Disabilities
- Adolescents (<18)
- Older Adults (≥60)
Current Selection:
All Road Users; All Social Groups
 Indicator Selection
Justice
- Equity
- Fairness
- Accessibility
Safety
Livability
Sustainability
Aesthetics
Comfort
- Thermal Comfort
- Physical Comfort
- Psychological Comfort
Walkability
Bikeability
Selected Indicators:
Justice; Safety; Livability; Sustainability; Aesthetics; Comfort; Walkability
 1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.

"Pedestrian activity on the street increases community vitality"

For the purpose of this study, physical attributes and condition are examined to understand the impact of walkability attributes on pedestrian’s comfort of walking. 2.3. Connectivity and accessibility Connectivity and accessibility are important criteria for pedestrian comfort (Hutabarat Lo, 2009; Vojnovic, 2006). Connectivity relates to the ease of moving from origins to destinations is the major factor influencing the pedestrian route choice (Kumar, 2010). The street networks need to be well connected with proper sidewalks to varied destination to encourage people to walk in the city. A well-planned street network has streets that are well linked to other modes of transportation (Southworth, 2005). The streets should also provide varied uses of buildings and spaces, good quality of paths, adequate width of walkways, clear signage. The street design creates the visual interest of the built environment. All of these elements are important to facilitate walking with ease. Accessibility is an important factor for walkability. A place is accessible when there is an equal opportunity for everybody to use public spaces. A normal person can be disabled if accessibility is not provided. On the other hand, even a wheelchair user, a blind person or an elderly are not disabled in an accessible environment. Street with a large amount of frontages taken up by parking makes pedestrian access to buildings more difficult by requiring pedestrians to cross the parking lot. According to Handy, Xinyu and Mokhtarian (2006), different physical settings may affect the walking pattern and route choice. For example, pedestrians who choose to walk may consider the distance to the destination as important to reduce the time consumed. They will prefer a place that has short walking distance and high connectivity walkways. In one way, the distance of walking should be minimized and connectivity should be maintained in order to reduce the time and cost of travel. The scholar suggests that proximity, connectivity and accessibility are significant criteria in encouraging walking activity. In this respect, this study highlights the current condition and accessibility of facilities, proximity of the places and continuity of the walkways in providing physical comfort and pleasant walking for visitor as pedestrians. 2.4. Safety of walking Safety is one of the determinants of a walkable environment. A safe pedestrian environment allows the pedestrians to walk comfortably and reduces the sense of fear from accident or crime. Southworth (2005) claimed that the quality of the walking environment might influence pedestrian intensity. The intensity of pedestrian is required to increase safety because the places become more transparent (Jacobs, 1969).
